It’s important to identify who benefits from a project and ensure they contribute to project costs. Giving regions flexibility in how they allocate costs within the region can also assist in obtaining broader stakeholder support and allow costs to be more accurately assigned to areas that receive the most benefit. However, given the complexities of trying to estimate project benefits and beneficiaries for individual stakeholders—especially over the long life of a transmission project–cost and benefit estimates do not have to be perfectly precise. Several strategies can reduce potential opposition to new projects, including quantifying and communicating the full range of project benefits, not just costs, and engaging with stakeholders and state champions to build external support. Bundling projects into a portfolio can identify a suite of projects that provide a broader distribution of benefits across the region, facilitating regional cost allocation. Finally, establishing a backstop method can help ensure cost-effective projects can go forward in case project-specific cost allocation agreements cannot be reached. The process to implement any of these lessons through changes to cost allocation methods is not simple. Each region has split authority to file cost allocation changes among multiple stakeholder groups. However, transmission providers now have an opportunity to engage stakeholders and implement changes as part of their compliance filing for FERC Order 1920.
